title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: It was a long time before Pierre could fall asleep that night. He paced up and down his room, one moment turning some difficult problem over in his mind and frowning, the next suddenly shrugging his shoulders and wincing, and then smiling happily.

He was thinking about Prince Andrew, about Natasha, about their love—one moment jealous of her past, the next reproaching himself for that very feeling. It was already six in the morning, and he was still pacing the room.

"Well, what am I supposed to do if it can't be avoided? What am I to do? It's clearly meant to be," he said to himself, and undressing hastily, got into bed—happy and agitated, but without a trace of hesitation or doubt.
"Strange, impossible as this kind of happiness seems, I have to do everything in my power so that she and I become husband and wife," he told himself.
A few days earlier Pierre had decided to leave for Petersburg on Friday. When he woke up on Thursday, Savelich came in to ask about packing for the trip.

"What, to Petersburg? What's Petersburg? Who's even in Petersburg?" he asked himself, though only inwardly. "Oh, right—a long time ago, before all this happened, I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he thought. "Why, though? Well, maybe I'll go anyway. What a good man he is, so attentive, remembering everything," he thought, looking at Savelich's old face, "and what a pleasant smile he has!"
"So, Savelich, you still don't want to accept your freedom?" Pierre asked him.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the late count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never once been wronged."
"And what about your children?"
"The children will get along just the same. With masters like this, a person can live."
"But what about my heirs?" said Pierre. "Suppose I suddenly get married... it could happen," he added with an involuntary smile.
"If I may say so, your excellency, that would be a fine thing."
"How easily he takes it," thought Pierre. "He has no idea how frightening it is, how dangerous. Too soon, or too late... it's terrible!"
"So what are your orders? Are you leaving tomorrow?" asked Savelich.

"No, I'll put it off for now. I'll let you know later. Forgive me for the trouble I've caused you," said Pierre, and seeing Savelich smile, he thought: "But how odd that he doesn't know there's no Petersburg for me now, that this other matter has to be settled first! But he probably knows it perfectly well, and is only pretending not to. Should I talk it over with him, see what he thinks?" Pierre wondered. "No—another time."
At breakfast Pierre told his cousin, the princess, that he had visited Princess Mary the day before and had met there—"Guess who? Natasha Rostova!"
The princess seemed to see nothing more remarkable in that than if he'd mentioned running into Anna Semyonovna.
"Do you know her?" Pierre asked.
"I've seen Princess Mary," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. It would be a very good thing for the Rostovs—they say the family's utterly ruined."
"No—I mean, do you actually know Natasha Rostova?"
"I heard about that business of hers at the time. It was a great pity."
"No, she either doesn't understand or she's pretending," Pierre thought. "Better not say anything more to her about it."
The princess had also had provisions packed for Pierre's journey.
"How kind everyone is," thought Pierre. "What's strange is that they should still bother with these things now, when it can't possibly matter to them anymore. And all for my sake!"
That same day the Chief of Police came to see Pierre, inviting him to send someone to the Faceted Palace to collect property that was to be returned to its owners that day.

"And this man too," thought Pierre, studying the Chief of Police's face. "What a fine-looking, kind officer. Imagine troubling himself over such trifles now! And people actually say he's dishonest, that he takes bribes. What nonsense! Besides, why shouldn't he take bribes? That's how he was raised, and everyone does it. But what a kind, pleasant face, and how he smiles when he looks at me."
Pierre went to Princess Mary's for dinner.

As he drove through the streets past the burned-out houses, he found himself struck by the beauty of the ruins. The jagged chimney stacks and crumbling walls of the burned quarters of the city, stretching out and half-hiding one another, reminded him of the Rhine and of the Colosseum. The cabmen he passed and their fares, the carpenters cutting timber for new houses with their axes, the women peddlers, the shopkeepers—all of them looked at him with bright, cheerful eyes that seemed to say: "Ah, there he is! Let's see what comes of it!"

At the entrance to Princess Mary's house Pierre found himself doubting whether he had really been there the night before, whether he had really seen and talked with Natasha. "Maybe I imagined it; maybe I'll walk in and there won't be anyone there." But he had barely stepped into the room before he felt her presence with his whole being, in the loss of his sense of freedom. She was wearing the same black dress with its soft folds, her hair done the same way as the day before, and yet she was completely different. If she had looked like this when he'd walked in the day before, he could not for a single moment have failed to recognize her.

She looked the way he had known her almost as a child, and later as Prince Andrew's fiancée. A bright, questioning light shone in her eyes, and her face wore a friendly, strangely mischievous expression.
Pierre had dinner with them and would have stayed the whole evening, but Princess Mary was going to vespers, so Pierre left the house along with her.

The next day he came early, had dinner, and stayed the whole evening. Though Princess Mary and Natasha were clearly glad to see their visitor, and though all of Pierre's interest was now centered on that house, by evening they had talked their way through everything, and the conversation kept drifting from one trivial topic to another and repeatedly breaking off. He stayed so long that Princess Mary and Natasha exchanged glances, clearly wondering when he would leave. Pierre noticed this but still couldn't go. He felt uneasy and embarrassed, but he sat on because he simply could not bring himself to get up and say goodbye.
Princess Mary, seeing no end to it, was the first to rise, and complaining of a headache, began saying good night.
"So you're off to Petersburg tomorrow?" she asked.

"No, I'm not going," Pierre answered quickly, in a tone of surprise, almost offense. "Yes... no... to Petersburg? Tomorrow—but I won't say goodbye just yet. I'll come by in case you have any errands for me," he said, standing in front of Princess Mary, turning red, but making no move to leave.

Natasha gave him her hand and went out. Princess Mary, instead of leaving, sank into an armchair and looked at him with a stern, searching gaze from her deep, radiant eyes. The tiredness she had shown so plainly before had vanished completely now. With a long, deep sigh, she seemed to be settling in for a long talk.
The moment Natasha left the room, Pierre's confusion and awkwardness vanished instantly, replaced by eager excitement. He quickly pulled an armchair closer to Princess Mary.

"Yes, I wanted to tell you," he said, answering her look as though she had spoken aloud. "Princess, help me! What should I do? Can I hope? Princess, my dear friend, listen! I know everything. I know I'm not worthy of her, I know it's impossible to speak of it now. But I want to be a brother to her. No—not that. I don't want that, I can't..."
He stopped and rubbed his face and eyes with his hands.

"Well," he went on, with a visible effort to control himself and put his thoughts in order. "I don't know when I began to love her, but I have loved her, and only her, my whole life, and I love her so much that I can't imagine life without her. I can't propose to her right now, but the thought that maybe someday she could be my wife—and that I might be letting that chance slip away... that chance... it's unbearable. Tell me, can I hope? Tell me what I should do, dear princess!" he added after a pause, and touched her hand when she didn't answer.
"I've been thinking over what you told me," Princess Mary answered. "Here's what I'll say. You're right that speaking to her of love right now..."

Princess Mary stopped herself. She had been about to say that speaking of love was out of the question, but she stopped, because she had seen from the sudden change in Natasha two days earlier that far from being hurt if Pierre spoke of his love, it was exactly what she wanted.
"Speaking to her now just wouldn't do," the princess said all the same.
"But what should I do?"
"Leave it to me," said Princess Mary. "I know..."
Pierre looked straight into Princess Mary's eyes.
"Well?... Well?..." he said.
"I know that she loves—will love you," Princess Mary corrected herself.
Before she had even finished the sentence, Pierre had leapt up and seized Princess Mary's hand with a startled expression.
"What makes you say that? You think I may hope? You really think...?"
"Yes, I think so," said Princess Mary, smiling. "Write to her parents, and leave the rest to me. I'll tell her when the time is right. I want it to happen, and my heart tells me it will."
"No, it can't be! How happy I am! But it can't be.... How happy I am! No, it can't be!" Pierre kept repeating, kissing Princess Mary's hands.
"Go to Petersburg—that will be for the best. And I'll write to you," she said.
"To Petersburg? Go there? Very well, I'll go. But may I come again tomorrow?"

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than she'd been the day before, but that day, whenever Pierre looked at her, he sometimes felt as if he were dissolving, as if neither he nor she existed at all anymore, as if nothing existed but happiness itself. "Is it possible? No, it can't be," he told himself with every glance, every gesture, every word that filled his soul with joy.
When, saying goodbye, he took her thin, slender hand, he couldn't help holding it a little longer than he should have.

"Is it possible that this hand, this face, these eyes, all this wealth of feminine charm that still feels so strange to me, is it possible that one day it will be mine forever, as familiar to me as I am to myself?... No, that's impossible!..."
"Goodbye, Count," she said aloud. "I'll look forward so much to your return," she added in a whisper.

And those simple words, her look, and the expression on her face as she said them, gave Pierre two months' worth of endless memories, interpretations, and happy daydreams. "'I'll look forward so much to your return....' Yes, yes, how exactly did she say it? Yes—'I'll look forward so much to your return.' Oh, how happy I am! What is happening to me? How happy I am!" Pierre kept saying to himself.
